nature-gov-011.title: Measuring the goals: targets and indicators
nature-gov-011.text: A goal means little unless someone can tell whether it is being met. For the SDGs, indicators are the measures decision-makers use to track each target. Outcome targets carry numbers, like 6.1. Targets about the means of getting there carry letters, like 6.a. For each indicator, an expert group tried to name a custodian agency to handle methods, data and reporting. A UN forum monitors the whole effort, and countries may file voluntary reviews of their progress. Critics worry about the sheer number of indicators and the cost of tracking them, estimated in the billions of dollars.

nature-gov-013.title: Are the SDGs too soft on the planet?
nature-gov-013.text: The SDGs treat economic growth as a foundation. Critics say that is the problem. In their view the goals never make protecting the Earth system an end in itself, and environmental limits, including the planet's safe boundaries, are underrepresented. Even within the environmental goals, most indicators measure social or economic results. Some studies argue that real planetary integrity and justice would require limits to growth. A 2022 review of over 3,000 articles found the SDGs had only limited power to transform politics. Many environmentalists want sustainable development redefined, against the goals' growth-centered design.

nature-gov-012.title: When the goals pull against each other
nature-gov-012.text: Can the world end hunger, grow economies and narrow income gaps while also protecting the environment? Critics doubt that all 17 SDGs can be reached together, because some work against others. They say the goals lean on doubtful claims that growth can be decoupled from resource use, instead of facing the tension head-on. Synergies exist too. The IPCC sees strong links between climate action and the goals on health, clean energy, cities, consumption and oceans. In practice, countries favor social and economic goals, with SDGs 1 and 8 the most widely prioritized. Scholars still disagree on whether the goals are coherent or built on conflicting targets.

nature-gov-016.title: The COP: the Biodiversity Convention's parliament
nature-gov-016.text: Every government that has ratified the Biodiversity Convention sits on its governing body, the Conference of the Parties, or COP. The COP reviews progress, sets priorities and work plans, and can amend the convention and create expert advisory bodies. One of these, the SBSTTA, advises it on science and technical matters. The first COP met in Nassau, Bahamas. Meetings ran yearly for three years after 1994, then every two years. COP 15, planned for Kunming in 2020, was delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic and split into two sessions.

nature-gov-024.title: The Kunming-Montreal framework: a Paris Agreement for nature
nature-gov-024.text: On 19 December 2022, nearly every country on Earth agreed a new plan for nature. The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework was adopted at the UN Biodiversity Conference, COP15, and promoted as a "Paris Agreement for Nature." It is the most significant agreement under the Biodiversity Convention so far. It replaced the plan that held the missed Aichi targets. It sets four global goals for 2050 and 23 targets for 2030. Goal A aims to cut the extinction rate and risk of all species tenfold by 2050 and halt human-caused extinctions of threatened species. Target 3, described in {{ref:nature-gov-033}}, asks governments to protect 30% of Earth's land and water by 2030. Countries are also to stop subsidizing activities that destroy wild places, such as mining and industrial fishing. Target 13 commits them to share fairly the benefits from genetic resources and their digital sequence data. The name tells a story. Kunming was the original host, but Montreal took over after China's COVID policy forced Kunming to withdraw. The framework is not legally binding. Critics, including the chair of IPBES, warn its vague targets may yield business as usual. By COP16, only 44 of 196 parties had new biodiversity plans.

nature-gov-033.title: 30 by 30: protecting a third of the planet
nature-gov-033.text: Protect 30% of Earth's land and ocean by 2030. The goal fits on a bumper sticker, and that is part of its power. It was proposed in a 2019 Science Advances article, "A Global Deal for Nature," partly to help slow climate change. The High Ambition Coalition launched it in 2020, and more than 100 countries backed it by October 2022. In December 2022 it became Target 3 of the global biodiversity framework. As of May 2026, 17.3% of land and inland waters and 9.8% of marine areas were protected. Counting conservation sites outside formal reserves, the shares were 18.4% and 10.0%. The number itself is disputed. Some conservationists say 30% lacks clear scientific backing, while others say it is too low and point to the Half-Earth idea of conserving about 50%. Critics warn loose definitions could count industrial areas and inflate progress. NGOs and Indigenous groups warn that without human-rights safeguards it could bring forced evictions and green colonialism, land seized in the name of nature.

nature-gov-019.title: A hard treaty gone soft: criticism of the Biodiversity Convention
nature-gov-019.text: Countries face no penalty for ignoring the Biodiversity Convention, which is why critics call it a hard treaty gone soft. Brazil argued that wealthy countries benefit from access to nature's resources but give too little money and technology for conservation. Developing countries and their allies dispute whether richer nations have met their obligations at all. National strategies in practice neglect groups such as fungi, bacteria and protists. Some scientists also fear its Nagoya Protocol hampers disease prevention and conservation research.

nature-gov-018.title: Mapping the ocean's most important places
nature-gov-018.text: Some patches of ocean matter far more to marine life than others. Under the Biodiversity Convention, scientists identify these Ecologically or Biologically Significant Marine Areas, or EBSAs, using scientific criteria. Expert workshops from 2018 to 2022 explored how to revise the descriptions and add new areas. The work feeds a binding instrument under the Law of the Sea for biodiversity beyond national waters: the High Seas Treaty.

nature-gov-056.title: The World Charter for Nature, 1982
nature-gov-056.text: On 28 October 1982 the UN adopted a declaration meant to guide all human conduct that affects nature. The vote was 111 for and 18 abstentions. The single vote against came from the United States. Prepared by the IUCN, the World Charter for Nature sets out five principles of conservation. They include respecting nature, protecting genetic viability and habitats, and managing resources for lasting productivity without endangering other species. It gave the first international recognition to a strong form of the precautionary principle.

nature-gov-039.title: Six kinds of protected area
nature-gov-039.text: "Protected area" covers everything from untouched wilderness to working landscapes. The IUCN's World Commission on Protected Areas sorts them into six categories by management goal. They run from Category Ia, the strict nature reserve, through Category II, the national park, to Category VI, where natural resources are used sustainably. Many governments and the UN recognize these categories as the international standard.

nature-gov-040.title: Do protected areas work?
nature-gov-040.text: Inside protected areas, vertebrate populations declined about 0.4% a year. At similar unprotected sites, they fell about 1.8% a year, roughly five times faster. Protected area effectiveness asks exactly this: how well reserves actually prevent biodiversity loss, judged for instance by comparing populations inside and outside. Small size, isolation, high costs and rising conflict over resources all limit what reserves achieve. And only 18% of the area under protection has been assessed, so most reserves' effectiveness is unclear.

nature-gov-048.title: Digital sequence information: genes as data
nature-gov-048.text: Digital sequence information, or DSI, is the placeholder policy term for such data, like DNA sequences drawn from genetic resources. It is crucial to medical, biological and breeding research. Researchers share it freely online. That clashes with benefit-sharing rules, because anyone can use it without an agreement. At COP 15 in 2022, parties agreed a shared mechanism that separates access from benefit-sharing. At COP 16 in 2024 they created the Cali Fund. Industries using DSI, like cosmetics, should pay in part of their profits, half going to local and Indigenous groups.

nature-gov-028.title: Paying fleets to empty the sea
nature-gov-028.text: Some government money pushes fishing fleets to grow too big, catch too much or fish illegally. These harmful fisheries subsidies are what SDG Target 14.6 aims to end. Subsidies that add capacity can help developing countries compete with large fishing nations. But they bring no lasting benefit if they cause overfishing. Illegal fishing alone costs up to $36.4 billion a year, by the WWF's estimate. The global biodiversity framework likewise asks countries to stop subsidizing destructive activities such as industrial fishing.

nature-gov-029.title: Giant marine reserves
nature-gov-029.text: Some marine protected areas are vast, at least 100,000 square km each. These large-scale reserves are set up to curb overfishing and human disturbance of ocean ecosystems. They raise hard questions about managing resources, rivalry between countries, and trade-offs between people's needs and nature. The biggest practical problem is policing them. Monitoring and enforcement of their protections are often inadequate.

nature-gov-044.title: The Cartagena Protocol: rules for moving modified organisms
nature-gov-044.text: Exporters shipping genetically modified corn or cotton must now label it. That rule comes from the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety, an add-on to the Biodiversity Convention that governs the movement of genetically modified organisms between countries. It was adopted on 29 January 2000 and entered into force on 11 September 2003. It rests on the precautionary principle from the 1992 Rio Declaration: lack of full scientific certainty is no reason to delay cost-effective protection. Countries may ban imports that lack evidence of safety. Importers can assess risks before the first shipment and weigh social and economic concerns.

nature-gov-045.title: The Bonn Convention: protecting animals that cross borders
nature-gov-045.text: A bird that breeds in one country and winters in another needs protection in both. The Convention on Migratory Species, also called the Bonn Convention, aims to conserve migratory animals across their whole range. It was signed in Bonn on 23 June 1979 and took effect on 1 November 1983, with a secretariat run by UNEP. Appendix I lists migratory species threatened with extinction, which range countries must strictly protect. Appendix II lists species that would gain from cooperation, the basis for regional deals. It has spawned seven agreements, including one covering 254 wetland bird species.

nature-gov-021.title: Climate and biodiversity: one crisis, two faces
nature-gov-021.text: Climate change and biodiversity loss feed each other, and fixing one can worsen the other if their links are ignored. In June 2021, IPBES and the IPCC released a joint workshop report making exactly that case. The two problems, it argued, must be tackled together.

nature-gov-023.title: The IPBES Nexus Assessment
nature-gov-023.text: Biodiversity, water, food, health and climate change are tangled together, so a fix for one can help or hurt the others. An IPBES report approved on 17 December 2024 studied those links. It looks for ways to get the greatest benefit across all five at once.

nature-gov-022.title: The IPBES Transformative Change Assessment
nature-gov-022.text: The 2019 IPBES Global Assessment reached a blunt conclusion. Only transformative change, a deep shift in how societies work, can achieve global development goals. It also warned against focusing solely on economic growth while biodiversity disappears. A follow-up report, approved on 18 December 2024, examined the underlying causes of biodiversity loss and how such change can be brought about.

nature-gov-032.title: Ending the illegal wildlife trade
nature-gov-032.text: Illegal wildlife trade has become one of the world's largest black markets, worth tens of billions of dollars. SDG targets 15.7 and 15.c aim to end poaching and trafficking of protected species by tackling both demand and supply. Trafficking is usually run by organized crime and helped by corruption and weak governance. Outright bans are not always the fastest remedy. Trade policies that reward sustainable use typically help wildlife populations recover faster.

nature-gov-025.title: What the biodiversity framework means for business
nature-gov-025.text: The global biodiversity framework is aimed at governments, but money will feel it too. According to the UNEP Finance Initiative, companies should expect mandatory disclosure of their impacts on nature. Banks are expected to move money into projects that restore nature, and central banks to treat nature loss as a risk within their mandate. The goal of halting and reversing nature loss by 2030, described in {{ref:nature-gov-079}}, has helped carry the framework into business. In May 2024, UNEP and China launched the Kunming Biodiversity Fund, with China committing $230 million USD.

nature-gov-035.title: The EU's biodiversity plan for 2030
nature-gov-035.text: On 20 May 2020 the European Commission set out its plan for nature, offered as Europe's contribution to the coming global framework. The EU Biodiversity Strategy for 2030 aims to protect 30% of EU territory by 2030, with 10% strictly protected. It proposed binding targets for restoring nature and is a core part of the European Green Deal. As of 2023, the EU was not on track to meet its targets.

nature-gov-034.title: Paper parks: protected only on the map
nature-gov-034.text: A reserve can exist in law and still be logged, poached and built on. Such paper parks lack the money, staff or enforcement to stop damage inside them. Modeling suggests that for exploited species, better enforcement in existing reserves often helps more than adding area without more resources. Where over-harvesting is intense, spending on management can beat creating new, weak reserves. Where threats cluster at reserve edges, though, enlarging an area can create a safe core even without more staff. Chasing percentage targets without the capacity to govern risks spreading scarce money too thin.

nature-gov-037.title: Red tape or fair play? Criticism of the Nagoya Protocol
nature-gov-037.text: Some developing countries have refused permits for basic biodiversity research, and some have even prosecuted scientists. Critics blame the Nagoya Protocol's bureaucracy for harming research, conservation and disease response. Its country-by-country permit system moves slowly. By contrast, the multilateral system of the treaty on plant genetic resources allows 8500 transfers every week. Weak national implementation is often blamed for the failure. Scientists and museums see red tape. Countries that supply genetic resources see protection against the theft of their genetic wealth.

nature-gov-050.title: The EU Nature Restoration Law
nature-gov-050.text: More than 80% of Europe's habitats are in poor condition. A 2024 EU regulation set binding targets to fix that. Member states must restore at least 30% of damaged habitats by 2030, 60% by 2040 and 90% by 2050. The aims include protecting ecosystem services, slowing climate change and reducing risks to food security. The law split Europe. Farm groups and the center-right European People's Party called it a threat to livelihoods, while scientists and the IUCN backed it. Parliament passed it 329 to 275, and it took effect on 18 August 2024.

nature-gov-058.title: National biodiversity strategies: the convention at home
nature-gov-058.text: Before COP16, countries were meant to present updated plans for meeting the Kunming-Montreal targets. Only 25 of 195 did. These plans are National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plans, or NBSAPs: each country's main plan for carrying out the Biodiversity Convention at home. The convention requires each country to prepare one and build it into planning in every sector that affects nature. As of early 2012, 173 parties had developed one. The late updates are telling. Only five of the 17 megadiverse countries, the richest in species, and four G7 nations met the deadline. Japan's 2023 plan includes the aim of an economy that restores more nature than it destroys.

nature-gov-054.title: The common heritage of humankind
nature-gov-054.text: Some resources, such as the deep seabed, are said to belong to all humanity rather than to any one nation. That is the common heritage principle. Before 1992, plant genetic resources were treated this way, freely exchanged for breeding and research. Developing countries objected that their resources were being exploited without payment. The Biodiversity Convention replaced the principle with national sovereignty. The tension returned in the High Seas Treaty talks, which turned on common heritage versus freedom of the seas. Rich and poor nations still disagree over which rule should apply.

nature-gov-042.title: The 2010 Biodiversity Target: a promise unkept
nature-gov-042.text: In June 2001, EU leaders meeting at Gothenburg set a goal: halt, or significantly slow, the decline of biodiversity by the end of 2010. In 2002 the Biodiversity Convention's sixth COP committed to a significant cut in the rate of loss by 2010. A world summit in Johannesburg confirmed it. Even measuring the rate of loss proved hard. The world largely failed. In 2010, 110 national reports showed little progress.

reviews.biodiversity-agreements-and-targets: The world has written many promises for nature, from the 1971 Ramsar wetlands treaty and the Biodiversity Convention to 17 SDGs and the Kunming-Montreal framework's 23 targets for 2030. Most bind no one, and the record shows it: the 2010 target and the Aichi targets were missed, and in 2024 only 17% of SDG targets were on track. Protected areas are the main tool, and inside them vertebrates decline more slowly, but many are paper parks, and the push for 30 by 30 raises fears of evictions. A second thread runs through the chapter: who owns the genes of living things, first common heritage, then national property under the Nagoya Protocol, and now open data in the Cali Fund era.
